strengths: The paper addresses a real theoretical gap in score-based generative modeling: existing Wasserstein analyses often require the forward time T1 to diverge, while this work gives a finite-T1 prediction-correction guarantee by adding an inexact Langevin corrector before the reverse ODE.

The main theorem is technically meaningful: it decomposes the sampling error into early stopping, score approximation along the reverse path, and Langevin initialization error, with T1 depending only logarithmically on dimension and the norm-subgaussian tail parameter rather than on the target sampling precision.

The assumptions on the data distribution are relatively mild for this literature. Norm-subgaussianity covers bounded data and many practical distributions, and the paper carefully explains why the perturbed distribution satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality after finite OU time.

The paper makes a useful effort to connect its stronger endpoint loss to the usual L2 score-matching objective via Theorem 4.2, using a truncation argument. This helps align the theory with what is optimized in practice.

Presentation is generally clear for a theory paper. The algorithmic idea, theorem statements, error terms, and proof roadmap are understandable, and the appendix appears to provide detailed supporting arguments.
weaknesses: The main guarantee is continuous-time. The paper explicitly leaves a rigorous convergence result for discretizing the reverse ODE to future work, so the claimed practical improvement for implementable samplers is only partially established.

The endpoint loss epsilon_MGF in Theorem 4.1 is substantially stronger than the standard L2 score loss. Theorem 4.2 mitigates this, but through a technical coordinate-wise truncation of the score at T1 and a stringent small-loss condition, whose practical relevance is not convincingly demonstrated.

The bound still depends on the one-sided Lipschitz behavior of the learned score through I_tau(t). Although the paper removes the previous asymptotic condition lim Ls(t) = -1, the resulting bound may be hard to evaluate or control for realistic neural score networks.

Empirical evidence is very limited: only toy 2D datasets are shown, with little experimental detail. There is no validation on realistic diffusion benchmarks, nor evidence that the proposed all-corrector-then-reverse strategy improves sample quality or compute in practice.

The discretization discussion for the Langevin corrector requires additional smoothness assumptions and treats several parameters as constants when deriving the O(1/epsilon^2 log(1/epsilon)) complexity. This makes comparison with prior discrete DDPM analyses somewhat suggestive rather than fully conclusive.

Reproducibility is adequate for the theoretical results, since proofs are included, but weak for the simulations: the manuscript does not appear to provide code, hyperparameters, estimator architectures, or enough detail to reproduce Figure 1 exactly.

The limitations and ethics discussion is minimal. Ethical concerns are not central for this theoretical contribution, but the paper could more explicitly delimit that the results do not yet provide an end-to-end practical sampler guarantee.

strengths: The paper addresses a real theoretical weakness in standard analyses of score-based diffusion models: the need to send the forward noising time T1 to infinity while score approximation and discretization errors worsen with large T1. Framing this as a finite-time prediction-correction procedure is a meaningful and relevant question.

The main theorem is clearly stated and decomposes the Wasserstein error into interpretable terms: early stopping, score approximation along the reverse process, and approximation of p_T1 by inexact Langevin dynamics. The use of log-Sobolev regularization of the OU-smoothed distribution gives a plausible route to finite-T1 guarantees.

The assumptions on the data distribution are relatively mild for a theory paper: norm-subgaussianity covers bounded data and many practical settings. The paper also makes a useful effort to connect the stronger exponential-moment loss at time T1 back to the usual L2 score-matching loss via a truncation argument.

The exposition is mostly clear. The relationship to prior convergence results in Wasserstein distance, KL/TV analyses, Schrödinger bridge approaches, and predictor-corrector sampling is explained well enough to situate the contribution.
weaknesses: The practical significance is overstated relative to the evidence. The main guarantees are continuous-time, while actual diffusion sampling is discrete. Section 6 only proves a partial result for the initial inexact Langevin stage and explicitly leaves the reverse ODE discretization analysis to future work, so the claimed improved discrete-time convergence is largely heuristic.

The proposed method adds a potentially expensive Langevin correction phase at time T1. The paper argues that increasing T2 is preferable to increasing T1, but it does not give a complete end-to-end computational comparison once score-network evaluation cost, Langevin steps, reverse ODE integration, and discretization errors are all included.

The convergence bound still depends on quantities that are difficult to control or verify for learned neural score models, especially the one-sided Lipschitz integral I_tau(t) and the additional technical condition involving limsup of exp(2∫Ls). The paper says the one-sided Lipschitz constant does not enter the bound in the same way as prior work, but it remains central through I_tau and can dominate the guarantee.

The bridge from realistic L2 score loss to the stronger MGF loss relies on a truncation of the score estimator at T1. The authors call this purely technical and do not use it in the simulations, but without it the MGF loss can diverge even when L2 error is small. This weakens the claim that the assumptions match practical score training.

The empirical component is extremely limited: only toy two-dimensional datasets are shown, with no detailed experimental protocol, no learned high-dimensional score models, no comparison against standard predictor-corrector samplers, and no runtime or sample-quality evaluation. For an ICML main-track paper making claims motivated by practical diffusion sampling, this is not enough supporting evidence.

The novelty is moderate rather than compelling. The paper combines known ingredients: OU smoothing, log-Sobolev inequalities for Gaussian convolutions, inexact Langevin convergence with estimated scores, and Wasserstein stability of reverse dynamics. The synthesis is useful, but the paper does not fully demonstrate that it leads to a practically actionable or broadly superior algorithm.

Reproducibility is incomplete for the numerical results. The manuscript does not provide enough detail about how the toy score estimators were trained, how W2 was estimated, what hyperparameters were used, or whether code will be released. The theoretical statements are detailed, but the experimental evidence is hard to independently assess.

The limitations discussion is too brief. Important limitations, including high-dimensional constants, sensitivity to learned-score Lipschitz behavior, the cost of Langevin correction, and the absence of a full discretized sampler theorem, are either downplayed or deferred rather than treated as central constraints on the contribution.

strengths: The paper identifies a real theoretical instability in existing SGM convergence analyses: taking the forward time T1 to infinity helps initialization but can worsen score/discretization errors. The proposed predictor-corrector variant gives a clean way to replace this with finite T1 plus Langevin correction at the terminal noise level.

The main Wasserstein convergence result is technically meaningful. Theorem 4.1 separates early stopping, score error, and initialization error, and the use of log-Sobolev regularization of the perturbed law gives a convincing explanation for why only logarithmic dependence on dimension/tail parameters is needed.

The assumptions on the data distribution are relatively mild for theory work: norm-subgaussianity covers bounded image-like data, and the score error is ultimately connected to the L2 score-matching loss used in practice via Theorem 4.2.

The manuscript is well organized and readable. It clearly positions itself relative to prior Wasserstein/KL analyses, explains the role of T1, T2, tau, and delta, and includes full proof details in the appendix.

The small numerical illustration supports the qualitative behavior predicted by the theory: increasing the Langevin correction time T2 decreases both W2(pT1,q0) and W2(p,p_theta) on toy distributions.
weaknesses: The main guarantee is continuous-time. The paper discusses discretization and gives a result for the inexact Langevin stage, but explicitly leaves rigorous convergence of the reverse ODE discretization to future work. This limits the direct reproducibility and practical applicability of the claimed sampling improvement.

The end-to-end connection to practical score training still relies on technical devices that may be nontrivial in real models. The MGF-type loss in Theorem 4.1 is stronger than L2, and Theorem 4.2 controls it through a coordinatewise truncation of the terminal score estimator that the experiments do not actually apply.

The quantitative bounds include constants and conditions that may be conservative, e.g. the lower bound on T1 in Theorem 4.2 scales with log(d(||X||SG+1)/delta), and the discretized Langevin proposition adds Lipschitz assumptions on both the true and estimated terminal scores.

The empirical section is very limited: only low-dimensional toy datasets are shown, with no comparison to standard predictor-corrector implementations or realistic diffusion benchmarks. This is acceptable for a theory paper, but it weakens claims about practical relevance.

The paper treats limitations only partially. It notes the missing reverse-ODE discretization analysis, but does not deeply discuss how restrictive the truncation, terminal-score regularity, or OU-only presentation may be in modern high-dimensional diffusion pipelines.

Reproducibility is adequate for the mathematics but thin for the simulations: the manuscript gives plots and qualitative descriptions, but not enough implementation detail to reproduce Figure 1 precisely. Research ethics concerns appear minimal because the work is theoretical and uses toy data.

strengths: The paper addresses a real theoretical instability in standard SGM analyses: prior convergence bounds often require the forward time T1 to grow, while score and discretization errors worsen with T1. The proposed two-stage predictor-corrector scheme gives a clean way to keep T1 finite by using inexact Langevin dynamics to sample approximately from p_T1 before running the reverse process.

The main Wasserstein result is technically meaningful. Theorem 4.1 separates early stopping error, score approximation error, and initialization error, and the use of log-Sobolev regularization of p_T1 after finite OU time is a convincing mechanism for exponential convergence of the correction stage.

The assumptions on the data distribution for the main continuous-time theorem are relatively mild for this literature: norm-subgaussianity rather than compact support, manifold regularity, or a functional inequality on the original data distribution.

The paper makes a useful effort to connect the stronger MGF-type score error needed for inexact Langevin analysis back to the L2 score loss minimized in practice via Theorem 4.2. This is an important bridge between the proof technique and realistic score training objectives.

The exposition is generally clear for a theoretical paper. The related work discussion explains well how the result differs from prior Wasserstein, KL/TV, and predictor-corrector analyses, and the proof sketches are helpful before the appendix.

The discretized TV result in Section 5 demonstrates that the algorithm can be combined with existing reverse-SDE discretization analyses, and it highlights a plausible complexity advantage from fixing T1 independently of the final accuracy.
weaknesses: The practical significance is not fully established. Empirical evidence is limited to small synthetic examples, with little detail on training, sample sizes, hyperparameters, or reproducibility. There is no demonstration that the proposed all-at-the-beginning correction is competitive with standard predictor-corrector samplers on realistic image or audio benchmarks.

The main continuous-time Wasserstein guarantee still depends on quantities that may be hard to control in practice, especially the integral involving the one-sided Lipschitz constants of the learned score and the MGF-type error at T1. The truncation argument in Theorem 4.2 is mathematically useful but appears technical and may not correspond to a practical neural sampler.

The discretized result is only in total variation and requires additional global smoothness/Lipschitz assumptions on the true score and the estimator. These assumptions are stronger than the main continuous-time assumptions and may fail for important data distributions, so the practical discrete-time theory is less broad than the headline contribution suggests.

The algorithmic tradeoff is not completely quantified in realistic terms. The method replaces large T1 with an inexact Langevin stage of length T2 or N2 steps, but the paper gives limited evidence about when this is computationally favorable in practice, especially relative to standard corrector steps interleaved throughout sampling.

Some bounds and constants are quite loose, and the sufficient lower bounds on T1 can still scale with dimension and subgaussian norm in ways that may be conservative. The paper would benefit from clearer interpretation of these parameter regimes.

There are several presentation and proofreading issues in the technical sections, such as apparent typos in Lemma 4.4/proof notation for the second moment and a direction typo involving KL in the proof discussion. These do not seem fatal, but they make the proofs harder to audit.

Limitations are only briefly discussed. The paper could more explicitly state that the strongest Wasserstein result is continuous-time, that the practical discretized theorem uses stronger assumptions, and that the numerical evidence is illustrative rather than validating real generative-model performance.

strengths: The paper targets a real theoretical issue in score-based diffusion models: standard analyses require the forward time T1 to grow, which can make score-estimation and discretization terms unstable. The proposed two-stage scheme, using terminal-time inexact Langevin dynamics before the reverse process, is a natural and potentially useful way to separate initialization error from reverse-process error.

The main technical route is coherent: the authors combine Wasserstein stability of the deterministic reverse flow, log-Sobolev regularization of the perturbed terminal distribution, and inexact Langevin convergence. The finite-T1 perspective is a meaningful conceptual contribution relative to analyses that initialize directly from the Gaussian prior.

The manuscript is generally readable and well organized. The related work section situates the paper against prior Wasserstein/KL/TV convergence results, and the appendix gives detailed proofs rather than only sketches.

The discretized TV result in Section 5 helps connect the continuous-time Wasserstein theorem to existing non-asymptotic diffusion analyses, even though it is not a full discretization of the main ODE result.
weaknesses: The practical significance is much weaker than the framing suggests. The proposed method replaces the need for large T1 with an additional Langevin sampling stage at time T1, and the paper does not convincingly establish that this is computationally preferable in realistic high-dimensional diffusion settings. The comparison is mostly by upper bounds, not by meaningful experiments or wall-clock/sample-quality tradeoffs.

The central claim that only standard L2 score loss is needed is only partially supported. Theorem 4.1 requires the stronger exponential-moment loss at time T1; Theorem 4.2 controls it only after a terminal-time clipping/truncation procedure and under a substantially larger T1 condition. The paper calls this truncation 'purely technical', but it is part of the proof mechanism and is not validated in realistic models.

Several assumptions remain restrictive or underspecified for practical neural score models. Assumption A1 requires global Lipschitz continuity and uses a one-sided Lipschitz integral inside the bound; convergence also needs an additional boundedness condition on this integral as JSM -> 0. The discrete result further assumes Lipschitzness of the true score over the whole interval and Lipschitzness of the learned terminal score, which weakens the 'minimal assumptions' narrative.

The theory is fragmented across metrics and algorithms. The main Wasserstein theorem is continuous-time and for the deterministic reverse ODE, while the implementable discretized theorem is in total variation and for the stochastic reverse SDE, relying heavily on prior analyses. Thus the paper does not give a complete discrete Wasserstein guarantee for its headline algorithm.

The empirical evidence is very thin: Figure 1 contains only toy 2D-style simulations with no implementation details, no baselines, no code/reproducibility information, and no high-dimensional generative modeling experiments. This is inadequate for supporting claims about practical benefits of choosing finite T1 or using the proposed predictor-corrector scheme.

The bounds include large constants and parameter constraints, for example in the log-Sobolev lower bound and the T1 requirements, and the discussion does not assess whether these regimes are meaningful for common diffusion-model scales. The logarithmic dependence is appealing asymptotically, but the usable quantitative message is unclear.

Limitations and ethics are not treated adequately. The paper has a short conclusion but no substantive limitations discussion about the gap between theory and practice, the cost of the added Langevin stage, sensitivity to score error tails, or applicability beyond OU/VP processes. Ethical issues are likely minor for a theory paper, but reproducibility and scope limitations should still be addressed.

strengths: The paper addresses a real gap in the theory of score-based generative models: prior Wasserstein and divergence analyses often require the forward perturbation time T1 to grow, while the proposed predictor-corrector scheme obtains convergence with fixed finite T1. This is a meaningful and well-motivated contribution.

The main technical results are substantial. Theorem 4.1 gives a Wasserstein bound for the continuous-time ODE reverse process, and the analysis cleanly decomposes early stopping, score-estimation, and initialization/correction errors. The use of log-Sobolev regularization of the perturbed distribution and inexact Langevin convergence is technically convincing.

The paper is careful about realistic score-estimation assumptions. Theorem 4.2 explicitly addresses the gap between standard L2 score loss and the stronger exponential-moment loss needed for inexact Langevin analysis, giving an end-to-end route from the practical training objective to the theorem.

The discretized-scheme discussion in Section 5 increases the usefulness of the contribution. Although it relies on existing reverse-SDE analyses, it shows that the finite-T1 idea can be combined with practical exponential-integrator sampling and yields improved dependence on the target accuracy compared with a standard reverse-SDE bound.

Presentation is generally strong for a theory paper: the motivation is clear, the relationship to prior and concurrent work is explicit, and proof sketches explain the main mechanisms before the detailed appendices. The assumptions and error terms are mostly stated transparently.

Reproducibility of the theoretical contribution is good: algorithms, assumptions, constants, and proofs are included in enough detail for a reader to check the claims. The toy simulations are secondary and consistent with the theory.
weaknesses: The empirical component is very limited. Figure 1 uses only low-dimensional toy distributions, and the paper does not demonstrate that the proposed beginning-only corrector improves practical high-dimensional diffusion sampling, compute, or sample quality. This is acceptable for a theory paper but limits the practical significance of the method.

The strongest Wasserstein result is for a continuous-time deterministic reverse ODE. The paper discusses discretization only in total variation for a stochastic reverse SDE by importing existing analyses; a discretized Wasserstein guarantee for the main ODE-style algorithm remains open.

Some assumptions remain nontrivial in practice. The quantitative dependence on one-sided Lipschitz constants through I_tau, the Lipschitz assumptions in the discretized result, and the need to control or enforce the exponential-moment loss at T1 may be hard to verify for neural score networks.

The truncation/correction in Theorem 4.2 is described as technical and not used in the toy experiments, but it is part of the formal route from L2 loss to the stronger loss. The paper could better clarify whether this modification is intended as an implementable algorithmic step or only as an analysis device, and what effect it would have in realistic models.

The limitations discussion is rather implicit. The manuscript acknowledges costs such as the stronger loss, early stopping, and reliance on existing discretization results, but it lacks a consolidated limitations section covering the absence of high-dimensional experiments, unresolved Wasserstein discretization, and practical verification of assumptions.

The manuscript appears to refer to prior online versions and later follow-up works, which is useful context but may create anonymization or positioning issues for a double-blind ICML submission if not handled according to the conference policy. No material ethical risks are apparent given the theoretical nature of the work.
